description: A timeline comparison of how BlackBerry’s fall accelerated—from enterprise dominance to near-collapse—as iPhone and Android reshaped the smartphone era.
youtube_description:
🎬 The Death of BlackBerry isn’t one moment—it’s a chain reaction. In this chart-race, we compare BlackBerry, Apple, Samsung, and Microsoft from 2007 through 2025, tracking the rapid rise of iPhone/Android and the enterprise-to-consumer shift that BlackBerry couldn’t outrun.

⏱️ Chapters:
0:00 — The enterprise giant (2007–2010)
1:05 — iPhone flips the design rules (2010–2012)
2:15 — Android accelerates, BlackBerry stumbles (2011–2013)
3:25 — The pivot era: Windows Phone + consolidation (2013–2016)
4:35 — BlackBerry becomes a brand, not a platform (2016–2019)
5:45 — Microsoft finds a new engine (Azure/cloud era)
6:50 — Apple + Samsung dominate the smartphone stack (2020–2025)

📌 What to watch for:
• The inflection point when smartphone growth moved from QWERTY-first to app-first.
• How market expectations transformed “hardware leadership” into “ecosystem leadership.”
• Why BlackBerry’s revenue trajectory diverged while Apple and Samsung scaled.

👍 Like, subscribe, and comment your pick: Which pivot mattered most—Apple’s 2007 iPhone launch, Android’s open wave, or Microsoft’s cloud turnaround?

instagram_caption:
🚀 The “QWERTY King” imploded—while iPhone and Android rewrote the rules in real time.

In 2007, BlackBerry wasn’t just another phone—it was the enterprise heartbeat. In our timeline, BlackBerry’s total value sits at about $7.4B, while the smartphone future is about to change overnight. The decisive shift starts with Apple. By 2008, Apple rises to ~$37.4B as the iPhone proves that consumers don’t just want messaging—they want an app-powered world.

Then Android hits the accelerator. From 2009 to 2011, Samsung’s rise is steep—moving from ~$30.3B to ~$75.0B—because it scales across brands and price points. BlackBerry, meanwhile, peaks around 2011 at ~$19.7B, but that’s the last big crest. From there the story turns brutal: by 2012, BlackBerry drops to ~$8.7B as the market moves from “email-first” to “ecosystem-first.”

Microsoft tries to stay relevant with Windows Phone, but the chart reveals the difference between an OS and a platform: Microsoft’s line continues upward overall, yet the Windows Phone bet can’t match the momentum Apple and Samsung lock in. BlackBerry slides further—~$5.9B (2013) → ~$4.4B (2014) → ~$1.2B (2016). By 2018–2019, it’s essentially a late-era comeback myth: the platform gravity is gone.

The final chapter (2020–2025) is dominance. Apple expands to ~$435B by 2025, Samsung reaches ~$305B, while Microsoft accelerates into its cloud era with ~$780B. BlackBerry ends up not “winning another version,” but surviving as a historical lesson.

Be honest: would BlackBerry have survived if it fully embraced touch + an app ecosystem sooner—or was the ecosystem shift always fatal?

Follow for more chart-race timelines—and subscribe so you don’t miss the next downfall-to-dominance story.
facebook_caption:
The smartphone market’s most dramatic pivot story is the decline of BlackBerry alongside the rise of iPhone and Android ecosystems. This timeline comparison tracks enterprise-to-consumer momentum from 2007 through 2025 across four key players.

BlackBerry’s peak arrives around 2011 (about $19.7B), reflecting its earlier dominance in corporate messaging and security. But the market’s center of gravity rapidly shifted toward app ecosystems and touch-first experiences. As Apple’s iPhone becomes the consumer benchmark (Apple grows from ~$20.2B in 2007 to ~$150.0B by 2012) and Android scales through Samsung (Samsung rises from ~$30.3B in 2009 to ~$90.0B by 2012), BlackBerry’s value trajectory declines sharply.

By 2016, BlackBerry falls to roughly $1.2B, demonstrating the cost of arriving late to the ecosystem era. Meanwhile, Microsoft’s overall growth reflects its successful repositioning toward cloud and enterprise software (rising to approximately $780B by 2025). The result is a stark chart-race: one company that defined an era loses the platform battle, while Apple and Samsung consolidate smartphone leadership.

Which lesson do you think was the hardest: ecosystem timing, UX shift to touch, or platform developer incentives?
